events_chronological: Dreading conscription, a young man and his closest friend agree to end their lives together; the friend dies and the young man is discovered still breathing.
The survivor is convicted over the death and taken away to serve a sentence.
A typist starts an affair with a soldier who has a wife at home, meeting him on packed trains and in unlit streets.
Steering an ambulance through a night of bombing, a woman in trousers pulls another woman out of a house that has come down.
The two women become lovers in the weeks that follow the rescue.
The pair share a flat, one of them jealous of everyone the other knew first and lying about small things.
The younger of the two meets an old lover of her partner's, and the two of them start an affair kept carefully hidden.
The typist bleeds badly after a backstreet termination in a hired room, and the soldier walks out and leaves her there.
The ambulance driver finds her bleeding, gets her to a hospital, and slides her own gold band onto the girl's finger so the nurses will assume a husband.
The convicted man shares a cell with an objector who keeps pressing him about what he is really being punished for.
The ambulance driver lodges alone in a rented room, walking the streets in men's clothes with nothing left to occupy her.
The two lovers live together while one of them goes through the other's pockets and letters hunting for a betrayal she cannot name.
The typist takes a desk at a marriage agency and still meets her soldier in hotel rooms, the borrowed gold band shut in a drawer.
The released man keeps house for an elderly lodger until the objector from his cell arrives at the door and unsettles the whole arrangement.
nonlinear_category_reason: Scene order runs from the latest stretch to the earliest throughout, with no present-day level the telling returns to. The three dated parts run 1947, 1944, 1941; each part moves forward inside itself, but every part is earlier than the one before it.
syuzhet_notes: The story is in three dated parts running backwards: the latest year first, then the middle years, then the earliest. The opening four bullets are the aftermath, the middle five the war years that produced it, and the last five the beginning of everything.
fabula_notes: Chronology is unambiguous because each part carries a date. Within a part the narration moves forward, so the reversal operates on the parts rather than on individual scenes.
